'''Daniel Charles Shanks''' (January 17, 1917 – September 6, 1996) was an [[Americans|American]] [[mathematician]] who worked primarily in [[numerical analysis]] and [[number theory]]. He was the first person [[numerical approximations of π|to compute π]] to 100,000 decimal places.

==Life and education==
Shanks  was born on January 17, 1917, in [[Chicago, Illinois]]. He is not related to the English mathematician [[William Shanks]], who was also known for his computation of π. He earned his [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in physics from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1937, and a [[Ph.D.]] in Mathematics from the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]] in 1954. Prior to obtaining his PhD, Shanks worked at the [[Aberdeen Proving Ground]] and the [[Naval Ordnance Laboratory]], first as a physicist and then as a mathematician. During this period he wrote his PhD thesis, which he completed in 1949, despite having never taken any graduate math courses.<ref name="Williams NAMS obit">{{cite journal|last = Williams|first = H. C.|date=August 1997|title = Daniel Shanks (1917–1996)|journal = Notices of the American Mathematical Society|volume = 44|issue = 7|pages = 813–816|publisher = American Mathematical Society|location = Providence, RI|bibcode = 1997MaCom..66..929W|issn = 0002-9920|url = https://www.ams.org/notices/199707/comm-shanks.pdf|access-date = 2008-06-27}}</ref>{{Rp|813}}

After earning his PhD in mathematics, Shanks continued working at the [[Naval Ordnance Laboratory]] and the Naval Ship Research and Development Center at [[David Taylor Model Basin]], where he stayed until 1976. He spent one year at the [[National Bureau of Standards]] before moving to the [[University of Maryland, College Park|University of Maryland]] as an adjunct professor. He remained in Maryland for the rest of his life.<ref name="Williams NAMS obit" />{{Rp|813}} Shanks died on September 6, 1996.<ref name="Williams NAMS obit" />{{Rp|813}}

==Works==
Shanks worked primarily in [[numerical analysis]] and [[number theory]]; however, he had many interests and also worked on [[black body]] radiation, [[ballistics]], [[mathematical identities]], and [[Epstein zeta function]]s.<ref name="Williams NAMS obit" />{{Rp|814}}

===Numerical analysis===
Shanks's most prominent work in numerical analysis was a collaboration with [[John Wrench]] and others to [[numerical approximations of π|compute the number π]] to 100,000 decimal digits on a computer.<ref name="Shanks & Wrench">{{cite journal|last = Shanks|first = Daniel|author2=John W. Wrench Jr.|author2-link=John Wrench|year = 1962|title = Calculation of π to 100,000 Decimals|journal = Mathematics of Computation|volume = 16|pages = 76–99|issn = 0025-5718|doi = 10.2307/2003813|issue = 77|jstor = 2003813|publisher = Mathematics of Computation, Vol. 16, No. 77}}</ref> This was done in 1961 on an [[IBM 7090]], and it was a major advancement over previous work.<ref name="Williams NAMS obit" />{{Rp|814}}

Shanks was an editor of the ''[[Mathematics of Computation]]'' from 1959 until his death.<ref name="EditorialBoard">{{cite web | title=Mathematics of Computation :: Past Editorial Board Members | website=American Mathematical Society | date=2024-07-15 | url=https://www.ams.org/publications/journals/journalsframework/mcom/editorial_history_mcom | access-date=2025-05-15}}</ref> He was noted for his very thorough reviews of papers, and for doing whatever was necessary to get the journal out.<ref name="Williams NAMS obit" />{{Rp|813}}

===Number theory===
Shanks wrote the book ''Solved and Unsolved Problems in Number Theory'',<ref name="SUPINT">{{cite book|last = Shanks|first = Daniel|title = Solved and Unsolved Problems in Number Theory|edition = 5th|publisher = AMS Chelsea|location = New York|year = 2002 |isbn = 978-0-8218-2824-3}}</ref> which mostly depended on [[quadratic residues]] and [[Pell's equation]]. The third edition of the book contains a long essay on judging conjectures,<ref name="SUPINT" />{{Rp|239 ff}} in which Shanks contended that unless there is a lot of evidence to suggest that something is true, it should not be classified as a conjecture, but rather as an open question. His essay provided many examples of bad thinking that were derived from premature conjecturing. Writing about the possible non-existence of odd [[perfect numbers]], which had been checked to 10<sup>50</sup>, he famously remarked that "10<sup>50</sup> is a long way from infinity."<ref name="SUPINT" />{{Rp|217}}

Most of Shanks's number theory work was in [[computational number theory]]. He developed a number of fast computer factorization methods based on [[quadratic forms]] and the [[class number (number theory)|class number]].<ref name="Williams NAMS obit" />{{Rp|815}} His [[algorithms]] include: [[Baby-step giant-step]] algorithm for computing the [[discrete logarithm]], which is useful in [[public-key cryptography]]; [[Shanks's square forms factorization]], [[integer factorization]] method that generalizes [[Fermat's factorization method]]; and the [[Tonelli–Shanks algorithm]] that finds square roots modulo a prime, which is useful for the [[quadratic sieve]] method of [[integer factorization]].

In 1974, Shanks and [[John Wrench]] did some of the first computer work on estimating the value of [[Brun's constant]], the sum of the reciprocals of the [[twin prime]]s, calculating it over the twin primes among the first two million primes.<ref name="Shanks & Wrench Brun's Constant">
